lead: An engine burns a mixture of petrol and air. The air-fuel ratio sets how completely that burn uses the fuel. It also sets how much carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbon and nitrogen oxide leave the tailpipe. The controller therefore cannot choose one ratio for all conditions: it must move between rich, stoichiometric and lean as the engine warms, accelerates or cruises. This chapter links combustion, the three-way catalyst, exhaust gas recirculation and fuel economy in litres per 100 km, km per litre and grams of carbon dioxide (CO2) per km.
prereq: You need 4.1 for the legal ceilings and first-year chemistry of complete and incomplete combustion; the oxygen sensor itself is covered in Unit 3, Exhaust gas oxygen (lambda) sensors.

blocks.text: Petrol needs about 14.7 kg of air for every 1 kg of fuel to burn completely. This is the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio, AFR<sub>st</sub>. The actual air-fuel ratio AFR is air mass divided by fuel mass. Lambda λ is AFR divided by AFR<sub>st</sub>. At λ = 1 the mixture is stoichiometric. λ < 1 is rich: not enough air for all the fuel. λ > 1 is lean: excess air.

The pollutants follow λ. CO (carbon monoxide) forms when fuel burns with too little oxygen, so CO rises sharply rich. HC (unburnt hydrocarbon) comes from flame quench at the cold cylinder wall, gas trapped in crevices and unburnt mixture; it too is high when rich. NOx (nitrogen oxides) forms when nitrogen and oxygen combine at high flame temperature and stay hot long enough. It is low rich, peaks slightly lean, then falls as the flame cools. Diesel PM (particulate matter) comes from fuel-rich spots inside a spray, even when the average diesel mixture is lean.

The figure plots relative CO, HC and NOx against λ. At λ = 1.0 it shows CO 35, HC 45 and NOx 60. At λ = 1.05 NOx reaches 85 while CO falls to 22. Only a narrow band near λ = 1 suits a three-way catalyst.

blocks.where: AFR is actual air mass per fuel mass in kg air per kg petrol; AFR<sub>st</sub> is 14.7 kg air per kg petrol; λ is dimensionless, with λ = 1 stoichiometric, λ < 1 rich and λ > 1 lean.

blocks.text: An oxidising catalyst uses exhaust oxygen to burn CO to CO2 and HC to CO2 and water. It lowers CO and HC but cannot remove NOx. A three-way catalyst also reduces NOx to nitrogen. It needs the exhaust to swing slightly rich and slightly lean around λ = 1: rich spells feed the reduction, lean spells feed the oxidation. Outside that window one pollutant always runs away.

The catalyst must be hot. Light-off temperature is about 250 to 350 °C. Below light-off conversion is poor, so the first minute after a cold start can carry much of a trip's emissions. The controller runs rich and retards spark to heat the catalyst, then returns to λ = 1.

EGR, exhaust gas recirculation, sends part of the exhaust back to the intake. The inert gas dilutes the charge and lowers peak combustion temperature, so NOx falls. At part load EGR has little effect on fuel economy and can slightly improve it by reducing pumping losses and allowing more spark advance. Excessive EGR slows combustion, can misfire and then does cost fuel. The ECU schedules EGR by speed and load and switches it off at idle and full load.

items: Oxidation: 2CO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub>; for a hydrocarbon C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>m</sub>: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>m</sub> + (n + m/4) O<sub>2</sub> → n CO<sub>2</sub> + (m/2) H<sub>2</sub>O.
Three-way: oxidation plus NOx reduction, but only inside the λ window.

blocks.text: Fuel economy has two common forms. km per litre is higher-is-better; litres per 100 km is lower-is-better. They are reciprocal: L/100 km = 100 ÷ (km/L). A car giving 14.7 km/L uses 100 ÷ 14.7 = 6.8 L/100 km.

The CO2 mass is fixed by the carbon content of the fuel; almost all of that carbon leaves as CO2, so CO2 scales with fuel burnt, while CO and HC come from incomplete combustion. Burning 1 kg of petrol makes about 3.16 kg of CO2. For grams of CO2 per km, take fuel mass per km in kg, multiply by 3.16, then multiply by 1000. Fuel economy and CO2 are two views of the same fuel flow.

The controller chooses a compromise at every operating point. Rich mixtures can give more power and lower NOx, but raise CO, HC and fuel use. Lean mixtures can save fuel at light load, but raise NOx and may misfire. EGR cuts NOx; at part load it has little effect on fuel economy and can slightly improve it by reducing pumping losses, but excessive EGR slows combustion, can misfire and then does cost fuel. The three-way catalyst forces steady cruise close to λ = 1, the only point where all three pollutants can be cleaned at once.

figure.caption: Relative CO, HC and NOx against lambda. CO and HC fall as the mixture leans, while NOx peaks just lean of lambda = 1, leaving only a narrow band for a three-way catalyst.

spec.aria: CO and HC fall as the mixture goes lean while NOx rises to a peak just lean of lambda equal to one, so only a narrow band near lambda equal to one suits a three-way catalyst.

examples.question: A car uses 6.8 L of petrol to cover 100 km. Petrol density is 0.74 kg/L and burning 1 kg of petrol makes about 3.16 kg of CO2. Find the fuel mass per 100 km, the fuel mass per km, the CO2 in g/km, and λ when the air-fuel ratio drops to 13.2:1 under acceleration.
steps: Fuel mass per 100 km = volume × density = 6.8 L × 0.74 kg/L = 5.032 kg per 100 km, rounded to 5.03 kg.
Fuel mass per km = 5.032 kg ÷ 100 = 0.05032 kg/km, rounded to 0.0503 kg/km.
CO2 mass per km = 0.05032 kg/km × 3.16 kg CO2 per kg fuel = 0.1590112 kg/km.
In grams: 0.1590112 kg/km × 1000 g/kg = 159.0112 g/km, rounded to 159 g/km.
At AFR = 13.2:1, λ = 13.2 ÷ 14.7 = 0.8979, rounded to 0.90. This is rich because λ < 1.
examples.answer: The car uses 5.03 kg of petrol per 100 km, or 0.0503 kg/km, and emits 159 g CO2/km. At 13.2:1 the mixture is rich with λ = 0.90.
examples.check:
vol = 6.8
dens = 0.74
kg100 = vol * dens
kgkm = kg100 / 100
co2_kgkm = kgkm * 3.16
co2_gkm = co2_kgkm * 1000
lam = 13.2 / 14.7
print(round(kg100, 2))
print(round(kgkm, 4))
print(round(co2_gkm, 1))
print(round(lam, 2))

traps: Treating λ and AFR as the same number. λ is dimensionless; AFR is kg air per kg fuel. λ = 1 means AFR = 14.7 for petrol, not 1:1.
Believing a three-way catalyst cleans any mixture. Outside its narrow window near λ = 1, CO or NOx runs away.
Forgetting light-off. A cold catalyst at 20 °C does almost nothing even at λ = 1; about 250 to 350 °C is needed.
Thinking rich is free NOx control. Rich lowers NOx but raises CO, HC and fuel use, and can overheat the catalyst.
Mixing CO2 with regulated pollutants. CO2 is a greenhouse gas tied to fuel carbon, not a CO/HC/NOx limit.

quiz.q: Define the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio for petrol and lambda.
quiz.a: AFR<sub>st</sub> = 14.7 kg air per kg petrol. λ = AFR ÷ AFR<sub>st</sub>, so λ = 1 at the stoichiometric mixture.

quiz.q: Why does NOx peak slightly lean rather than very rich?
quiz.a: A rich mixture lacks excess oxygen. A very lean flame is cooler. The peak needs both high flame temperature and some excess oxygen, so it occurs slightly lean.

quiz.q: A car uses 7.5 L/100 km. Petrol density is 0.74 kg/L and 1 kg petrol makes 3.16 kg CO2. Find g CO2/km.
Why is a three-way catalyst ineffective outside the λ = 1 window?
quiz.a: Outside the window the exhaust lacks the right oxidising and reducing balance. Lean exhaust leaves NOx unreacted; rich exhaust leaves CO and HC unreacted. One pollutant always escapes.

quiz.q: How does EGR lower NOx and what is its effect on fuel economy?
quiz.a: EGR dilutes the intake charge and lowers peak combustion temperature. At part load it has little effect on fuel economy and can slightly improve it by reducing pumping losses, but excessive EGR slows combustion, can cause misfire and then does cost fuel.
About 250 to 350 °C, the temperature above which catalyst conversion becomes effective.

quiz.q: An engine runs at AFR 15.5:1. Find λ and state rich or lean.
quiz.a: λ = 15.5 ÷ 14.7 = 1.054. Since λ > 1, the mixture is lean.

quiz.q: Why are cold-start emissions high even with a good three-way catalyst?
quiz.a: The catalyst is below light-off, so conversion is poor. The warm-up mixture is often rich, raising CO and HC until the catalyst heats and closed-loop λ = 1 begins.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines use wideband lambda sensors, close-coupled catalysts, gasoline particulate filters, cooled EGR and model-based torque structures to hold λ and cut cold-start emissions. CO2 rules now push downsized turbo engines, mild hybrid stop-start and 48 V systems. Research directions include lean NOx traps, selective catalytic reduction for lean petrol, and real-driving emission control. Search next for three-way catalyst window, catalyst light-off, cooled EGR, WLTP and Bharat Stage VI OBD.
